title: Knife basics: tomato & onion salad
desc: Fifteen minutes of practice — claw grip, onion dice, garlic, herbs — that ends in a salad you eat.
left: Spoon over grilled halloumi or fish the next day.
trouble: Keep the root end on — it holds the layers together.
Put a damp cloth under it.

steps.t: Set up: board on a damp cloth, sharp chef's knife, a bowl for scraps. Hold the knife with the pinch grip and curl the fingertips of your other hand into a claw.
steps.w: A stable board and a pinch grip give control; the claw keeps fingertips behind the knuckles, which guide the blade.
steps.c: Knuckles touch the flat of the blade; the board doesn't move.
steps.m: Holding the knife by the handle only — it wobbles. Pinch the blade.
steps.img: hands holding a chef's knife with a pinch grip over a wooden board, claw grip on the other hand

steps.t: Dice the half red onion: cut through the root, peel, make 3–4 thin cuts towards the root without cutting through it, then slice across into small cubes.
steps.w: The uncut root holds the layers, so the cubes come out even.
steps.c: Small even cubes, about 5 mm.
steps.m: Cutting through the root first — the onion falls apart.
steps.img: halved red onion with vertical cuts held by its root on a board

steps.t: Crush the garlic clove with the flat of the knife, peel it, chop it, then add a pinch of salt and keep rocking the knife over it until it is a paste.
steps.w: Salt is abrasive and draws out juice, turning garlic into a paste that spreads evenly.
steps.c: A smooth, slightly wet paste.
steps.m: Lifting the knife tip off the board — keep the tip down and rock.
steps.img: garlic paste on a board under the flat of a chef's knife

steps.t: Cut the tomatoes into wedges, then into bite-size chunks. Pick the parsley leaves, bunch them and slice finely once — do not chop it to dust.
steps.w: A sharp single pass cuts herbs cleanly; hacking bruises them and they go black.
steps.c: Tomato chunks hold their shape; parsley is bright green.
steps.m: A blunt knife squashes the tomato — the skin should cut, not burst.
steps.img: tomato wedges and finely sliced parsley on a board

steps.t: Mix tomatoes, onion, garlic paste and parsley in a bowl with the olive oil, lemon juice and oregano. Taste, add salt until the tomatoes taste brighter.
steps.w: Salt draws juice out of the tomatoes, which mixes with oil and lemon into a dressing.
steps.c: A little juice pools at the bottom after a minute.
steps.m: Salting an hour early — the salad goes watery. Salt just before eating.
steps.img: a bowl of tomato onion parsley salad glistening with olive oil

title: Perfect fluffy basmati rice
desc: The absorption method: rinsed rice, measured water, lid on, then rest. Separate grains every time.
reheat: Microwave with a splash of water, covered, until steaming hot throughout. Reheat only once.
left: Next-day fried rice (cook from fridge-cold rice within 24 h).
trouble: Rinse until the water runs nearly clear; don't stir while it cooks.
Lid wasn't tight or heat too high — add 2 tbsp boiling water, lid on, 5 min more on lowest heat.
Heat too high — the lowest flame is enough once the lid is on.

steps.t: Rinse the rice in a sieve under cold water, swishing with your hand, until the water runs almost clear (about 1 minute).
steps.w: Rinsing removes loose surface starch, which is what glues grains together.
steps.c: Water draining through is nearly clear, not milky.
steps.m: Skipping the rinse — the rice turns sticky.
steps.img: basmati rice being rinsed in a fine sieve under a running tap

steps.t: Put rice, 225 ml water — 1.5 × the rice weight — salt and butter in a small saucepan. Bring to the boil on high heat.
steps.w: Basmati absorbs about 1.5 times its weight in water; measured water means nothing to drain.
steps.c: Water bubbling across the whole surface.
steps.m: Using a cup of water by eye — weigh it or measure it.
steps.img: small saucepan with rice and water starting to boil

steps.t: As soon as it boils, put the lid on, turn the heat to the lowest setting and cook 12 minutes. Do not lift the lid.
steps.w: The trapped steam cooks the grains evenly; lifting the lid lets it escape.
steps.c: Gentle hiss from under the lid, no rattling.
steps.m: Peeking — every lift lets the steam out.
steps.img: saucepan with a closed lid on a low flame

steps.t: Turn off the heat and leave it covered for 5 minutes, then fluff with a fork.
steps.w: Resting lets the moisture spread evenly so the top grains finish cooking.
steps.c: Little steam holes on the surface, every grain separate.
steps.m: Stirring with a spoon — it breaks grains. Use a fork.
steps.img: fluffy basmati rice being fluffed with a fork in a saucepan

steps.t: Leftovers: spread on a plate to cool, into the fridge within 1 hour, eat within 24 hours.
steps.w: Cooked rice can carry Bacillus cereus spores whose toxins form if it sits warm (FSA guidance).
steps.c: Rice cold within an hour.
steps.m: Leaving the pan on the hob overnight.
steps.img: cooked rice spread thinly on a plate to cool

title: Eggs three ways: soft-boiled, scrambled, fried
desc: Heat control in its simplest form. A 6½-minute egg, creamy low-heat scrambled eggs, and a fried egg with a set white.
trouble: Heat too high — take the pan off the heat while they are still slightly wet.
Lower eggs in gently with a spoon; fridge-cold eggs crack more.

steps.t: Soft-boiled: bring a small pan of water to a rolling boil. Lower 2 eggs in with a spoon and boil 6½ minutes.
steps.w: Timed boiling sets the white fully while the yolk stays runny.
steps.c: Big bubbles keep going after the eggs go in.
steps.m: Starting the timer before the water comes back to the boil.
steps.img: eggs being lowered with a spoon into boiling water

steps.t: Lift the eggs into a bowl of cold water for 1 minute, then crack the top and eat.
steps.w: Cold water stops the cooking so the yolk stays runny.
steps.c: Yolk runny, white set.
steps.m: Leaving them in the hot water.
steps.img: soft-boiled egg in an egg cup with a runny yolk

steps.t: Scrambled: whisk 2 eggs with a pinch of salt. Melt half the butter in a non-stick pan on LOW heat, pour the eggs in and stir slowly with a spatula, scraping the bottom.
steps.w: Low heat sets the proteins gently into soft curds; high heat squeezes out water and makes them rubbery.
steps.c: Soft folds form slowly over 3–4 minutes.
steps.m: High heat — dry, squeaky eggs.
steps.img: soft creamy scrambled eggs being folded with a spatula in a pan

steps.t: Take the pan off the heat while the eggs still look a little wet; they finish cooking on the plate. Pepper and parsley.
steps.w: Carry-over heat keeps cooking them for 30 seconds.
steps.c: Glossy, just set.
steps.m: Cooking until they look dry in the pan.
steps.img: glossy scrambled eggs on a plate with black pepper

steps.t: Fried: heat the remaining butter in the pan on medium, crack in 2 eggs, cook 3 minutes, spooning the hot butter over the white near the yolk.
steps.w: Basting sets the thick white around the yolk without flipping.
steps.c: White fully set and opaque, edges lightly golden, yolk still bright.
steps.m: Too hot — burnt lacy edges before the white is set.
steps.img: two eggs frying in butter in a pan, butter being spooned over

title: Spaghetti aglio e olio
desc: Salted pasta water and the trick of emulsifying it with oil into a silky sauce. Five ingredients.
trouble: Add more hot pasta water and toss hard — the starch binds oil and water.
Garlic burned — keep the heat medium-low and pull it at pale gold.

steps.t: Bring 2 litres of water to the boil with 20 g salt — it should taste like the sea.
steps.w: Pasta absorbs the water as it cooks; this is the only chance to season it from inside.
steps.c: Rolling boil, tastes clearly salty.
steps.m: A pinch of salt — bland pasta whatever sauce you add.
steps.img: large pot of boiling water with salt being added

steps.t: Add the spaghetti, stir for the first minute, and cook 1 minute less than the packet says.
steps.w: It finishes cooking in the pan with the sauce.
steps.c: Bite still has a thin white core.
steps.m: Not stirring early — strands glue together.
steps.img: spaghetti cooking in boiling water

steps.t: Meanwhile put the oil and sliced garlic in a cold pan, then heat on medium-low until the garlic is pale gold. Add the chilli flakes.
steps.w: Starting cold flavours the oil gently; garlic turns bitter if it browns.
steps.c: Garlic sizzles softly and turns pale gold in 3–4 minutes.
steps.m: Hot pan — the garlic burns in seconds.
steps.img: sliced garlic sizzling gently in olive oil, pale golden

steps.t: Scoop out a mug of pasta water, then lift the spaghetti straight into the garlic pan with tongs. Add 100 ml pasta water and toss hard for 1–2 minutes.
steps.w: Starch in the water emulsifies with the oil into a creamy sauce that clings.
steps.c: Sauce turns cloudy and silky and coats every strand.
steps.m: Draining all the water away in the sink.
steps.img: tossing spaghetti in a pan with garlic oil and pasta water, glossy sauce

steps.t: Off the heat, add parsley and parmesan; toss, loosen with a splash more water if it tightens, serve at once.
steps.w: Cheese melts into the emulsion off the heat without clumping.
steps.c: Glossy, loose, not oily.
steps.m: Adding cheese on high heat — it goes stringy.
steps.img: plate of spaghetti aglio e olio with parsley and parmesan

title: Béchamel
desc: White roux + milk. The base of cheese sauce, moussaka and lasagne. The milk-free version uses cream and water — see the variant.
reheat: Warm gently, whisking in a splash of liquid.
left: Make cheese sauce, top a gratin of cauliflower.
variant: The milk-free version: replace the milk with 150 ml cream + 350 ml water or unsweetened almond drink. Same method.
trouble: Whisk hard or blitz with a stick blender, then pass through a sieve.
Whisk in warm milk a splash at a time.
Simmer a few minutes longer, stirring.
Cook it longer — at least 5 minutes of simmering after the milk goes in.
goes: Moussaka, lasagne, cauliflower cheese, croque monsieur.

steps.t: Warm the milk with the bay leaf in a jug in the microwave or a pan until steaming, not boiling.
steps.w: Warm milk blends into the roux faster and with fewer lumps.
steps.c: Steaming, small bubbles at the edge.
steps.m: Boiling it over — watch it.
steps.img: a jug of steaming milk with a bay leaf

steps.t: Melt the butter in a saucepan on medium heat, add the flour and stir with a whisk for 2 minutes.
steps.w: Cooking the flour in fat coats the starch grains so they swell evenly later and removes the raw taste.
steps.c: A pale, bubbling paste that smells like biscuits, no colour.
steps.m: Letting it brown — béchamel should be white.
steps.img: white roux bubbling in a saucepan with a whisk

steps.t: Take out the bay leaf. Pour in a third of the milk and whisk hard until smooth and thick, then add the rest in two more goes, whisking each time.
steps.w: Adding liquid gradually lets each addition fully combine before the next — no lumps.
steps.c: Smooth, like thin custard, no lumps.
steps.m: Pouring it all in at once and stirring with a spoon.
steps.img: milk being whisked into a roux in a saucepan, smooth sauce forming

steps.t: Simmer gently 5–8 minutes, whisking often and scraping the corners. Season with salt and a few scrapes of nutmeg.
steps.w: Starch needs time at a simmer to thicken fully and lose its floury taste.
steps.c: Coats the back of a spoon; a finger line stays clear.
steps.m: Not scraping the corners — it catches and burns there.
steps.img: thick glossy bechamel coating the back of a wooden spoon

steps.t: If not using straight away, press baking paper onto the surface.
steps.w: Stops a skin forming.
steps.c: No skin after 10 minutes.
steps.m: Leaving it uncovered.
steps.img: bechamel in a saucepan covered directly with baking paper

title: Chicken velouté
desc: A blond roux thickened with stock instead of milk — silky, savoury, the base of mushroom and herb sauces.
left: Stir in mushrooms and cream for a quick chicken sauce.
trouble: Stock cubes — add unsalted water and a squeeze of lemon.
goes: Poached or roast chicken, fish, vegetables.

steps.t: Heat the stock until hot.
steps.w: Hot stock into the roux blends smoothly.
steps.c: Steaming.
steps.m: Cold stock straight from the fridge — slower and lumpier.
steps.img: golden chicken stock heating in a saucepan

steps.t: Melt the butter, add the flour and cook, whisking, 3–4 minutes until it smells nutty and turns pale blond.
steps.w: A blond roux has more flavour than a white one and suits stock.
steps.c: Colour of sand, nutty smell.
steps.m: Walking away — it goes from blond to burnt fast.
steps.img: blond roux in a saucepan, pale sand colour

steps.t: Whisk in the hot stock in three goes until smooth.
steps.w: Gradual addition prevents lumps.
steps.c: Smooth and slightly thick.
steps.m: All at once.
steps.img: stock whisked into roux, smooth velvety sauce

steps.t: Simmer 10 minutes on low, whisking now and then, skimming any skin. Season with lemon, salt only if needed, and pepper.
steps.w: Simmering cooks out the flour taste and reduces it to a velvety consistency.
steps.c: Coats a spoon like single cream.
steps.m: Salting before tasting — stock may already be salty.
steps.img: velvety veloute sauce coating a spoon

title: Quick espagnole (brown sauce)
desc: Browned vegetables, a brown roux, beef stock and tomato paste — the deep sauce behind classic steakhouse gravies.
left: Freeze in ice-cube trays: one cube upgrades any pan sauce.
trouble: The roux or vegetables burned — brown, not black.
Stock cubes: add water and a squeeze of lemon.

steps.t: Melt the butter in a saucepan and cook the onion, carrot and celery on medium for 8–10 minutes until golden brown.
steps.w: Browned vegetables add the sweet, roasted depth a brown sauce needs.
steps.c: Edges golden brown, smells sweet.
steps.m: Heat too high — black bits make it bitter.
steps.img: diced onion carrot and celery browning in butter in a saucepan

steps.t: Stir in the flour and cook 4–5 minutes, stirring, until it turns hazelnut brown.
steps.w: A brown roux thickens less but tastes deep and toasty.
steps.c: Colour of milk chocolate.
steps.m: Burning — stir constantly, scrape the bottom.
steps.img: brown roux with vegetables in a saucepan

steps.t: Stir in the tomato paste for 1 minute, then whisk in the hot stock gradually. Add bay and thyme.
steps.w: Frying the paste caramelises its sugars for colour and depth.
steps.c: Smooth dark sauce starting to bubble.
steps.m: Adding cold stock in one go — lumps.
steps.img: beef stock whisked into brown roux with tomato paste

steps.t: Simmer gently 25 minutes, skimming the surface, until reduced by about a third.
steps.w: Reduction concentrates flavour; skimming removes fat and impurities for a cleaner sauce.
steps.c: Coats a spoon, glossy brown.
steps.m: Hard boiling — it turns cloudy and greasy.
steps.img: dark brown sauce reducing in a saucepan, glossy

steps.t: Pour through a sieve, pressing the vegetables, and season with pepper.
steps.w: Straining gives a smooth finish.
steps.c: Smooth, glossy, coats a spoon.
steps.m: Salting before reducing.
steps.img: brown sauce being strained through a fine sieve

title: Classic tomato sauce
desc: Olive oil, garlic, tinned tomatoes, basil, time. The base for pasta, parmigiana, meatballs and shakshuka.
left: Shakshuka for breakfast, meatballs, pizza base.
trouble: Simmer longer and add a knob of butter — no sugar needed.
Add garlic on medium-low and don't let it brown.

steps.t: Sweat the onion in the olive oil with a pinch of salt on medium for 8 minutes.
steps.w: Slow-cooked onion adds sweetness that balances tomato acidity.
steps.c: Soft, see-through, no colour.
steps.m: Rushing on high heat — browned, harsh onion.
steps.img: translucent diced onion in olive oil in a pan

steps.t: Add the garlic and cook 1 minute until fragrant.
steps.w: Garlic needs only a minute; longer and it turns bitter.
steps.c: Smells strongly of garlic, still pale.
steps.m: Browning it.
steps.img: sliced garlic added to softened onions in a pan

steps.t: Tip in the tomatoes, rinse each tin with a splash of water into the pan, add the basil stalks and salt. Simmer uncovered 20 minutes, stirring now and then.
steps.w: Simmering evaporates water and cooks off the tinny taste.
steps.c: Thick enough that a spoon drawn through leaves a trail; oil shines on top.
steps.m: Lid on — it stays watery.
steps.img: tomato sauce simmering in a wide pan

steps.t: Take out the stalks, stir in the butter and torn basil leaves, taste and adjust salt.
steps.w: A little butter rounds off acidity without sugar.
steps.c: Glossy, sweet-sour, deep red.
steps.m: Adding sugar — not needed.
steps.img: glossy tomato sauce with torn basil leaves

title: Hollandaise by hand
desc: Egg yolks and butter whisked over steam into a warm emulsion. The skill: gentle heat.
reheat: Do not reheat directly; whisk over warm water.
left: Spoon over asparagus, salmon or eggs the next morning.
trouble: Whisk 1 tbsp hot water (or a fresh yolk) in a clean bowl and slowly whisk the split sauce into it.
Too hot — sieve it and keep the bowl off the water more often.
Whisk in a teaspoon of warm water.

steps.t: Melt the butter and keep it warm. Bring 3 cm of water to a bare simmer in a saucepan.
steps.w: Warm (not hot) butter emulsifies; boiling water below would scramble the yolks.
steps.c: Water only shivering, not bubbling.
steps.m: A rolling boil.
steps.img: melted butter in a jug next to a saucepan of gently simmering water

steps.t: Separate the eggs: yolks in a heatproof bowl (save whites in the fridge). Whisk the yolks with the water and lemon juice.
steps.w: Water and acid help the emulsion and slow the yolks from setting.
steps.c: Pale and frothy.
steps.m: Yolk with bits of white — fine, but shell bits are not.
steps.img: egg yolks being whisked with lemon juice in a glass bowl

steps.t: Set the bowl over the simmering water (not touching it) and whisk constantly for 2–3 minutes until thick and pale.
steps.w: Gentle heat thickens the yolks into a foam (the sabayon) that can hold the butter.
steps.c: Ribbon trail when the whisk is lifted; bowl warm but comfortable to touch.
steps.m: Leaving the bowl on too long — scrambled egg. Lift it off every 20 seconds.
steps.img: thick pale yellow egg yolk foam being whisked in a bowl over a pan

steps.t: Off the heat, whisk in the warm butter drop by drop, then in a thin stream, until thick and glossy.
steps.w: Fat added slowly is broken into tiny droplets surrounded by yolk — an emulsion.
steps.c: Thick, glossy, holds a soft shape.
steps.m: Pouring the butter in fast — it splits.
steps.img: melted butter poured in a thin stream into whisked yolks, glossy hollandaise

steps.t: Season with salt and more lemon to taste. Keep warm over the turned-off pan and use within 30 minutes.
steps.w: Above about 65 °C it splits, below it sets — warm is the zone.
steps.c: Pourable but thick.
steps.m: Putting it back on the heat.
steps.img: bowl of finished hollandaise with a spoon
